What Do Tabular Foundation Models Compute
In Context?
In-Situ Representation Refinement through
Attention-Gated Updates

Tian Zhou Affiliation: Ant Group    Beverly Jin Affiliation: Independent Researcher*Equal contribution    Linxiao Yang Affiliation: Ant Group    Xue Wang Affiliation: Independent Researcher*Equal contribution    Wenwei Wang Affiliation: Ant Group    Bingqing Peng Affiliation: Ant Group    Mengni Ye Affiliation: Independent Researcher*Equal contribution    Jinjie Gu Affiliation: Ant Group    Liang Sun Affiliation: Ant Group
Abstract

What reusable computation should a tabular foundation model learn when every table defines a new supervised task? We develop in-situ representation refinement: support labels guide updates to the episode’s representations, and these updates transfer to unlabeled queries without changing model parameters. A regularized leave-one-out objective yields a support correction and its query extension. The leading term separates attention-based reading from state-dependent scaling, motivating RefineICL: an attention-gated, FFN-free contextual stack with selected low-rank feature interaction and typed memory. RefineICL-L24 reaches 0.93836 OVR-AUC and 0.87173 accuracy on AMLB29. A benchmark-informed continuation reaches 1644.8 Elo on the 38-dataset TabArena snapshot, 31.4 Elo above TabPFN-3 under the same evaluation. It also improves all four reported metrics over TabPFN-v3 on both TabZilla views. In a matched 100K-update depth grid, an expanded FFN gives no consistent validation benefit and uses 60.2% more peak inference memory at L8. Internal interventions show that support representations are more than a static source of labels: removing one intermediate support update, while preserving the query output, increases final query cross-entropy in all 72 tested episodes. Together, the derivation and interventions explain how attention-gated updates can construct a task-specific predictor in context.

1 Introduction

Tabular foundation models turn supervised learning into a forward-pass computation: labeled rows are supplied as context and a pretrained network predicts the remaining rows (Müller et al., 2022; Hollmann et al., 2025; Qu et al., 2025). Their rapid empirical progress raises a more basic question than benchmark rank: what reusable computation converts a labeled table into its predictor?

In language modeling, Transformer feed-forward networks (FFNs) can act as parameterized key–value memories (Geva et al., 2021). A tabular episode has a different source of task information: feature meanings, class identities, and the decision boundary can all change, while task-specific supervision is supplied by the support rows. Parameters can therefore encode a procedure for recovering predictors across tables, while the context defines the predictor for the current table.

Existing views of in-context learning as optimization show that Transformers can emulate gradient-based or closed-form predictor updates in restricted settings (von Oswald et al., 2023; Akyürek et al., 2023). We make this view constructive for multiclass tabular ICL: rather than posit an optimizer in parameter space, we derive how labeled examples can reshape the representations of the current episode. We define a class-separation objective on the support representations. A regularized local optimization of this leave-one-out supervised neighborhood objective yields support corrections; a kernel extension gives the following approximate update for query state zqz_{q} and support states {zi}i=1n\{z_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}:

u⁡(zq)≃1α​∑iκ⁡(zq,zi)​fi,u(z_{q})\simeq\frac{1}{\alpha}\sum_{i}\kappa(z_{q},z_{i})f_{i}, (1)

where the kernel κ⁡(zq,zi)\kappa(z_{q},z_{i}) determines how much support example ii influences the query, and fif_{i} is an update vector determined jointly by support labels, neighborhood error, and the current representation; α>0\alpha>0 controls the regularization of this correction. Because fif_{i} depends on the other labeled rows, it cannot generally be computed from an isolated feature–label pair. This motivates updating support representations before reusing them for query prediction: support states are part of the computation, not just fixed examples to retrieve. Attention reads the resulting information, a gate scales its effect on the receiving state, and a residual connection applies the update. Depth then refines both the support representation and the query prediction, rather than repeatedly reading the same fixed support features.

The resulting architecture, RefineICL, learns this attention-gated update without a standalone expanded FFN. For tabular inputs, low-rank feature interaction constructs feature crosses before row compression, and typed memory restores feature-level information. The FFN-free stack retains strong contextual learning without paying the memory cost of expansion: in a matched 100K-update grid, expansion produces no consistent validation gain across L2/L4/L8 and raises peak inference memory by 60.2% at L8.

This account makes concrete experimental questions possible: do support updates help later query prediction, does their effect depend on the receiving state, and how do depth, representation width, and labeled context contribute? We test these questions with paired inputs and internal-state interventions.

Our contributions are:

  • •

    We formulate tabular ICL as in-situ representation refinement and derive a support update guaranteed to decrease this objective, together with an extension to unseen queries. The correction depends on support-label agreement and current neighborhood error. Its leading-order form separates reading that correction from controlling its strength, providing a constructive basis for attention-gated residual blocks.

  • •

    We turn this update structure into RefineICL, an attention-gated model with an FFN-free contextual stack, selected low-rank feature interaction, and typed memory. RefineICL-L24 checkpoints reach 0.93836 OVR-AUC and 0.87173 accuracy on AMLB29 and 1644.8 Elo after benchmark-informed continuation on TabArena, 31.4 Elo above TabPFN-3 under the same evaluation, and improves accuracy, F1, AUC, and log loss over TabPFN-v3 on both the 36-task and 102-task TabZilla views. A matched depth-by-FFN grid shows no consistent validation gain from expansion; adding it at L8 increases peak inference memory by 60.2%.

  • •

    We show that updating the support representations contributes to subsequent prediction. Preserving a middle block’s query output but skipping its support update increases final query cross-entropy in 72/72 episodes, by 0.0510 on average. Later blocks improve unlabeled-query nearest-prototype accuracy by 2.77 points; paired interventions further test the roles of update assignment, representation dimensions, and distinct labeled examples.

2 Related Work

ICL as an optimization algorithm.

Transformers can implement gradient descent, preconditioned updates, and closed-form linear predictors in context (von Oswald et al., 2023; Akyürek et al., 2023). These results establish an important optimizer view of ICL, while subsequent work questions whether a literal gradient-descent equivalence transfers to pretrained models outside those controlled settings (Shen et al., 2024). We complement the optimizer view by studying updates to episode representations rather than predictor parameters. Our objective follows supervised neighborhood learning (Goldberger et al., 2004; Frosst et al., 2019); the contribution is its regularized support correction, extension to unlabeled queries, and use in model design.

Conditional interaction versus standalone FFNs.

Transformer FFNs have been analyzed as parameterized key–value memories (Geva et al., 2021). Recommendation models instead emphasize efficient explicit feature interaction: DCN and DCN-V2 construct bounded-degree and low-rank feature crosses (Wang et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2021), while HSTU fuses contextual aggregation with multiplicative gating (Zhai et al., 2024). RefineICL uses selected low-rank feature interaction before row compression and an attention-gated update within the contextual stack. Its distinguishing contribution is the episode-representation account that motivates these operations, together with tests of how support labels, query state, and depth affect the learned update.

Tabular foundation models.

Prior-data fitted networks amortize Bayesian-style prediction over synthetic tasks (Müller et al., 2022). TabPFNv2 established strong small-data performance (Hollmann et al., 2025), and subsequent systems extend table scale, training distributions, and test-time computation (Grinsztajn et al., 2025; Grinsztajn et al., 2026). TabICL separates column representation from row-level inference (Qu et al., 2025; Qu et al., 2026); TabFM scales alternating feature and row computation (Google Research, 2026); and EXAONE-Tabular demonstrates that compact interleaved architectures remain competitive (Eo et al., 2026). We study how a pretrained model uses labeled rows to form a new predictor, using controlled experiments on internal states in the medium-scale regime.

Evaluation.

We retain each public benchmark’s dataset list and aggregation rule (Erickson et al., 2025; Bischl et al., 2021; Gijsbers et al., 2024; Grinsztajn et al., 2022; McElfresh et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2025).

3 In-Situ Representation Refinement

An episode supplies labeled support rows 𝒮={(xi,yi)}i=1n\mathcal{S}=\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n} and unlabeled query rows 𝒬={xj}j=n+1n+m\mathcal{Q}=\{x_{j}\}_{j=n+1}^{n+m}. To compute pθ​(yj∣𝒮,xj)p_{\theta}(y_{j}\mid\mathcal{S},x_{j}) without updating θ\theta, we study how support labels can refine the episode representation (Figures 1B and 2) and transfer that refinement to queries. Thus tabular ICL constructs an episode-specific predictor by updating labeled representations and transferring the resulting correction to each query: the support set is part of the computation, not only a collection to retrieve.

3.1 What makes a representation useful for this episode?

Labels define a local geometric target (Figure 2A).

Predict each support row from the other labeled rows. Let Z=[z1,…,zn]∈ℝd×nZ=[z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}]\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n} be the current support states, yi∈{1,…,C}y_{i}\in\{1,\ldots,C\}, and κ⁡(zi,zj)=exp⁡(τ​zi⊤​zj)\kappa(z_{i},z_{j})=\exp(\tau z_{i}^{\top}z_{j}) their similarity, where τ>0\tau>0 is an inverse temperature. For j≠ij\neq i, define

ai​j(Z)=κ⁡(zi,zj)∑k≠iκ⁡(zi,zk),qi(Z)=∑j≠iai​j(Z)𝟙[yj=yi].a_{ij}(Z)=\frac{\kappa(z_{i},z_{j})}{\sum_{k\neq i}\kappa(z_{i},z_{k})},\qquad q_{i}(Z)=\sum_{j\neq i}a_{ij}(Z)\mathbb{1}[y_{j}=y_{i}]. (2)

The correct-class neighbor mass qiq_{i} excludes self-votes: only the other support rows contribute to its prediction. With at least two support rows per class, the following loss is finite:

𝒥(Z)=−1n∑ilogqi(Z).\mathcal{J}(Z)=-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\log q_{i}(Z). (3)

This uses the soft-neighbor objective of supervised metric learning (Goldberger et al., 2004; Frosst et al., 2019). We optimize the episode states, derive a regularized correction, and extend it to queries; model inference remains a single forward pass.

Support labels determine an update direction.

The descent direction F=−∇Z𝒥​(Z)=[f1,…,fn]F=-\nabla_{Z}\mathcal{J}(Z)=[f_{1},\ldots,f_{n}] combines support states according to similarity, label agreement, and neighborhood error. Thus fif_{i} is not a fixed encoding of yiy_{i}: it changes as the episode’s representation changes. We smooth this direction using support similarity, so similar support states receive similar corrections.

Let K=[κ⁡(zi,zj)]i​j+ϵ​In≻0K=[\kappa(z_{i},z_{j})]_{ij}+\epsilon I_{n}\succ 0 be the support Gram matrix with a small diagonal term ϵ>0\epsilon>0, where InI_{n} is the n×nn\times n identity, and let α>0\alpha>0 be its regularization strength. If 𝒥\mathcal{J} is β\beta-smooth on a neighborhood containing the update segment, where β\beta is the smoothness constant, the regularized local objective in Appendix A has support-state solution U∗∈ℝd×nU^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n} satisfying

3.2 How does the correction reach an unlabeled query?

Similarity transfers the correction (Figure 2B).

For query state zqz_{q}, define kq=[κ⁡(zq,z1),…,κ⁡(zq,zn)]⊤k_{q}=[\kappa(z_{q},z_{1}),\ldots,\kappa(z_{q},z_{n})]^{\top}. The smooth kernel extension of the support correction is

u⁡(zq)=F​(β​K+α​In)−1​kq.u(z_{q})=F(\beta K+\alpha I_{n})^{-1}k_{q}. (6)

Its leading term when β​∥K∥2/α\beta\lVert K\rVert_{2}/\alpha is small is

u⁡(zq)≈1α​∑iκ⁡(zq,zi)⏟how much to read​fi⏟what correction to carry.u(z_{q})\approx\frac{1}{\alpha}\sum_{i}\underbrace{\kappa(z_{q},z_{i})}_{\text{how much to read}}\underbrace{f_{i}}_{\text{what correction to carry}}. (7)

Support labels determine fif_{i}; query similarity determines its influence, without a query label. Appendix B establishes consistency with the support update.

The leading-order update can be written as follows. Let

s⁡(zq)\displaystyle s(z_{q}) =∑jκ⁡(zq,zj),\displaystyle=\sum_{j}\kappa(z_{q},z_{j}), ai​(zq)\displaystyle a_{i}(z_{q}) =κ⁡(zq,zi)s⁡(zq),\displaystyle=\frac{\kappa(z_{q},z_{i})}{s(z_{q})}, (8)
r⁡(zq)\displaystyle r(z_{q}) =∑iai​(zq)​fi,\displaystyle=\sum_{i}a_{i}(z_{q})f_{i}, u⁡(zq)\displaystyle u(z_{q}) ≈s⁡(zq)α​r​(zq).\displaystyle\approx\frac{s(z_{q})}{\alpha}r(z_{q}).

The coefficients ai​(zq)a_{i}(z_{q}) are nonnegative and sum to one; equivalently, they are softmax attention weights with logits log⁡κ⁡(zq,zi)\log\kappa(z_{q},z_{i}). Hence r⁡(zq)r(z_{q}) has the form of attention over the support updates fif_{i}. The normalization removes the total similarity s⁡(zq)s(z_{q}), but the derived update still multiplies the result by the query-dependent scale s⁡(zq)/αs(z_{q})/\alpha. The update therefore separates where and what to read from how strongly to apply it.

3.3 How does this computation guide a neural block?

Read, scale, and update (Figure 2C).

The equations suggest two interacting branches. Attention reads a correction from the evolving support states, while a state-dependent gate controls how strongly the receiving state applies it. RefineICL uses a vector-valued SiLU gate so that this scaling can differ across representation dimensions. Their product is projected and added to the residual state:

hℓ+1=hℓ+Wo,ℓ​[Norm⁡(Aℓ​(h¯ℓ))⏟attention output⊙SiLU⁡(Wg,ℓ​h¯ℓ)⏟query-dependent gate]⏟residual correction.h_{\ell+1}=h_{\ell}+\underbrace{W_{o,\ell}\!\left[\underbrace{\operatorname{Norm}(A_{\ell}(\bar{h}_{\ell}))}_{\text{attention output}}\odot\underbrace{\operatorname{SiLU}(W_{g,\ell}\bar{h}_{\ell})}_{\text{query-dependent gate}}\right]}_{\text{residual correction}}. (9)

The scalar scale motivates the learned vector gate; the block need not compute the analytic correction exactly. Here hℓh_{\ell} collects the residual states at block ℓ\ell and h¯ℓ=LayerNorm⁡(hℓ)\bar{h}_{\ell}=\operatorname{LayerNorm}(h_{\ell}) is fed to both branches; Aℓ​(h¯ℓ)A_{\ell}(\bar{h}_{\ell}) is the learned attention readout; Norm\operatorname{Norm} is its normalization; Wg,ℓW_{g,\ell} and Wo,ℓW_{o,\ell} are the gate and output projections; and ⊙\odot is elementwise multiplication.

Three design consequences.

Update the support states: the correction fif_{i} depends on the current neighborhood, not just the label, motivating support updates before later query reads. Separate reading from scaling: attention normalizes relative similarities, while a gate controls the correction applied to the receiving state. Use the product as the nonlinear update: this computation does not require a separate expanded FFN. Section 6 tests these choices through support-update removal, query-specific attention/gate interventions, and the performance–memory cost of FFN expansion, respectively.

Three resources of the same update.

Depth applies more updates; width provides dimensions for task-specific updates; context supplies the labeled examples that define them. Section 6.2 tests these roles by measuring changes across layers, limiting the available dimensions, varying the number of support rows.

4 RefineICL: Attention-Gated Representation Refinement

4.1 Architecture

Figure 1C combines the theory-motivated contextual block with tabular feature processing; Appendix Figure 6 gives the full topology.

Attention-gated contextual refinement.

Every contextual block implements Equation 9: AℓA_{\ell} selects and combines information from the support rows, gℓ=SiLU⁡(Wg,ℓ​h¯ℓ)g_{\ell}=\operatorname{SiLU}(W_{g,\ell}\bar{h}_{\ell}) scales each feature, and Wo,ℓW_{o,\ell} adds the result to the residual state. This product supplies nonlinearity without a post-attention expanded FFN.

Selected low-rank feature interaction.

Because row compression can discard feature relations needed by later updates, a target-aware encoder first represents numerical values, categorical identity, and missingness separately. Two feature-graph rounds score candidate feature pairs; only the 16 strongest neighbors of feature ii contribute to its update:

mi=∑j∈𝒩16​(i)pi​j​WoFI​[(WuFI​hi)⊙(WvFI​hj)],hi′=hi+γFI​mi.m_{i}=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{N}_{16}(i)}p_{ij}W_{o}^{\mathrm{FI}}\left[(W_{u}^{\mathrm{FI}}h_{i})\odot(W_{v}^{\mathrm{FI}}h_{j})\right],\qquad h_{i}^{\prime}=h_{i}+\gamma_{\mathrm{FI}}m_{i}. (10)

Here hih_{i} is feature ii’s state, 𝒩16​(i)\mathcal{N}_{16}(i) contains its 16 highest-scoring partners, pi​jp_{ij} is the normalized selected-edge weight, WuFI,WvFI,WoFIW_{u}^{\mathrm{FI}},W_{v}^{\mathrm{FI}},W_{o}^{\mathrm{FI}} are learned low-rank projections, and γFI\gamma_{\mathrm{FI}} scales the residual update. All feature pairs are scored, but messages are computed only on selected edges; pre-compression and row-encoder interactions use ranks 32 and 64, respectively.

Row compression and typed-memory re-entry.

A three-block row encoder and RowCLS tokens compress a variable feature set into fixed-width row states. To recover feature-specific evidence later, RefineICL stores the feature states after two interaction rounds before RowCLS and retrieves them with eight-head gated reads at relative depths 1/31/3 and 2/32/3. Each read is initialized at zero and limited to 0.250.25 of the current row-state RMS. This restores feature-level information after compression without carrying all feature tokens through the stack. Component tests find a larger effect for gating than for memory and individual feature interactions (Appendix F.3).

4.2 Model sizes

L12 and L24 use feature embedding dimension 256, with (12,2048)(12,2048) and (24,1024)(24,1024) contextual (depth,width)(\text{depth},\text{width}). The controlled FFN comparison in Section 6.1 holds depth and width fixed while toggling the expanded FFN.

5 Experimental Design

Public benchmarks.

We evaluate L12 and L24 without dataset-specific updates. AMLB29, CC18, Grinsztajn, and TabZilla use saved splits and four members; TabArena uses its 38-dataset, eight-member snapshot. Appendix D gives the protocols; the code supplement provides code and training recipes.

Mechanism tests.

Fixed episodes test layerwise class separation, representation dimensions, and nested support sets. Query permutations preserve the vectors and their value distributions but change their recipients. We use paired bootstrap intervals; Appendix E defines each measure and control.

Controlled FFN comparison.

Matched d=96d=96 models train at L2/L4/L8 for 100K updates with a shared seed, toggling FFN-2×\times in column, row, and contextual blocks together. We compare held-out validation and, at L8, 54 boundary-rule conditions with 128–1,024 support rows and peak inference memory (Appendix E.5).

Component ablations.

We disable one model component at inference on identical inputs; a matched recovery study tests compensation (Appendix F.3). Paired comparisons measure how much each component affects the trained model.

6 Results

Benchmarks and FFN comparisons test predictive quality and memory cost. Internal interventions test whether support updates benefit later queries and whether attention and gating apply query-specific corrections. Depth, width, and context experiments examine the resources available to this computation.

6.1 Accuracy and efficiency of RefineICL

On AMLB29, L24 achieves 0.87173 accuracy and 0.93836 OVR-AUC, improving over L12 by 1.51 and 0.84 points and over TabPFN-v3 by 0.30 and 0.22 points. A benchmark-informed continuation reaches 1644.8 Elo on TabArena, 31.4 above TabPFN-3 under the same evaluation.

Table 2A extends the comparison to CC18, Grinsztajn, and TabZilla. L24 improves AUC over TabPFN-v3 on 27/36 TabZilla Canonical datasets and 68/102 Extension datasets (paired analysis in Appendix D.6). Its 159.5M parameters are 9.7% of TabFM’s 1.639B (Appendix Table 8).

The FFN-free model achieves strong prediction without separate expansion layers. Whole-model FFN expansion worsens CE at L2 and L4; its L8 gain costs 60.2% more peak memory. A separate 1,024-row boundary-rule probe gives the L8 FFN a 1.11-point accuracy gain (Appendix E.6). The complete validation grid and component deletion/recovery tests appear in Appendices E.5 and F.3.

6.2 Depth, width, and evidence scale contextual refinement

Depth repeats the update, width provides its representation dimensions, and labeled rows define the task. Figure 3 tests these roles through changes to the inputs or hidden states.

Depth improves predictions from the task representation.

On 72 held-out RBF episodes, each class prototype is the normalized mean of its labeled support states. Within one L24 forward pass, blocks 12–24 increase a query’s correct-versus-wrong prototype margin by 0.0509 (95% CI [0.0403, 0.0616]) and nearest-prototype accuracy by 2.77 points; query labels are never supplied. Support states include their labels; scoring excludes self-votes. Learned updates reduce this objective, whereas row-permuted updates increase it (Appendix E.2).

Later queries benefit from updated support states.

We preserve block 12’s query output, replace its support output with its input, and run later blocks normally. Final query CE increases in all 72 episodes, by 0.0510 on average (95% CI [0.0417, 0.0608]); accuracy falls by 1.44 points. Thus updating support representations improves later predictions even when the current query output is preserved (Appendix E.2).

Width provides dimensions for task-specific updates.

Keeping eight input features fixed, we broaden the labeling rule with the first BB eigenfunctions of the support RBF kernel. Projecting the 1,024-dimensional state after block 4 to rank 32 raises projection loss from 1.04 points at B=4B=4 to 8.66 at B=64B=64 (increase 7.62; 95% CI [6.03, 9.05]): broader rules use more representation dimensions.

Additional labeled rows widen the L24–L12 gap.

Across 72 matched task cells and fixed queries, nested support sets grow from 128 to 1,024 rows. L24 gains 23.86 points versus L12’s 19.85; their gap widens from 0.24 to 4.25 points (increase 4.01; 95% CI [2.26, 5.79]).

6.3 Support labels and query-specific updates

Figure 4 tests the two roles exposed by the theory: support labels select the episode-specific rule, while attention and gating route and apply its correction to each query. Model parameters remain unchanged in both tests.

Labels select which predictor the model uses (Figure 4B).

On identical support and query coordinates, we change only support labels among linear, XOR, radial, and wave rules, then score against all four query labelings. Matching cells average 0.985 accuracy versus 0.515 off the diagonal: labels switch the rule used on an unchanged point cloud.

Each correction is specific to its query (Figure 4A).

We permute the attention output, gate, or their paired update across queries before residual addition. The paired test preserves both vectors but assigns them to the wrong query. At 1,024 rows, accuracy drops by 52.28, 34.27, and 56.89 points, respectively: the rule is applied through query-specific updates. Component recovery appears in Appendix F.3.

Conclusion.

We develop tabular ICL as learning in the current episode’s representation space: support labels define a correction, similarity transfers it to queries, and repeated updates revise the task information used for prediction. Separating correction reading from state-dependent scaling motivates RefineICL’s attention-gated, FFN-free stack. It reaches 1644.8 TabArena Elo and improves all four reported metrics over TabPFN-v3 on both TabZilla views. Support-update interventions show that later queries benefit from evolving support states, while query-permutation tests establish the importance of attention/gate assignment. The derivation identifies a useful update structure; the experiments show how its components contribute to prediction and where FFN-free implementation saves memory.

Appendix: questions and evidence

The appendix follows the claims in the main text. Each experiment pairs its protocol with the quantity that answers the corresponding question; incomplete evaluations do not enter comparative claims.

Reviewer question Where to look What the evidence establishes
Does the derived update decrease the objective and extend to queries? Sections A–B Local improvement of the support objective and a controlled kernel approximation
Which operations are learned choices? Section C Connection to attention, gating, and residual updates; full architecture
Do the benchmark comparisons use compatible settings? Section D Dataset list, split and ensemble budgets; completed results
What do depth, working width and evidence change? Section E Paired class-separation, dimension-limit, and context-size measurements

Where does the refinement account fail? Section G Sparse identification, nonmonotone readouts and misleading raw rank

Appendix A Why the Support Update Decreases the Objective

The question is whether the proposed support correction improves the stated objective. We hold the current gradient and kernel fixed and assume local smoothness along the update segment; the bound below concerns support geometry, not unseen-label risk. For the exponential-dot-product kernel, the columns of F=−∇Z𝒥​(Z)F=-\nabla_{Z}\mathcal{J}(Z) are

Appendix B Extending Support Updates to Unseen Queries

Equation 6 follows from a vector-valued RKHS problem, which makes explicit why a correction learned on support representations can be evaluated at an unseen query. Let ℋκ~d\mathcal{H}_{\widetilde{\kappa}}^{d} be the product RKHS on indexed states z¯=(z,t)\bar{z}=(z,t), with κ~((z,t),(z′,t′))=κ(z,z′)+ϵ𝟙[t=t′]\widetilde{\kappa}((z,t),(z^{\prime},t^{\prime}))=\kappa(z,z^{\prime})+\epsilon\mathbb{1}[t=t^{\prime}]. Each support row and unseen query has a distinct index. Thus the support Gram matrix is exactly KK with its diagonal term, while unseen-query cross-kernels contain no such term. This convention also covers repeated feature vectors. Let g:(ℝd×ℐ)→ℝdg:(\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{I})\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d}, writing g⁡(zi)g(z_{i}) for its evaluation at support index ii. For the support corrections F=[f1,…,fn]F=[f_{1},\ldots,f_{n}], consider

ming∈ℋκ~d−∑i=1n⟨fi,g⁡(zi)⟩+β2​∑i=1n∥g⁡(zi)∥22+α2​∥g∥ℋκ~d2.\min_{g\in\mathcal{H}_{\widetilde{\kappa}}^{d}}-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\langle f_{i},g(z_{i})\rangle+\frac{\beta}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lVert g(z_{i})\rVert_{2}^{2}+\frac{\alpha}{2}\lVert g\rVert_{\mathcal{H}_{\widetilde{\kappa}}^{d}}^{2}. (16)

By the representer theorem, the minimizer has the form g⁡(⋅)=Γ​k⋅g(\cdot)=\Gamma k_{\cdot}, where kz=[κ~​(z¯,z¯1),…,κ~​(z¯,z¯n)]⊤k_{z}=[\widetilde{\kappa}(\bar{z},\bar{z}_{1}),\ldots,\widetilde{\kappa}(\bar{z},\bar{z}_{n})]^{\top} and Γ∈ℝd×n\Gamma\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n}. Substitution gives

−tr⁡(F⊤​Γ​K)+β2​∥Γ​K∥F2+α2​tr⁡(Γ​K​Γ⊤).-\operatorname{tr}(F^{\top}\Gamma K)+\frac{\beta}{2}\lVert\Gamma K\rVert_{F}^{2}+\frac{\alpha}{2}\operatorname{tr}(\Gamma K\Gamma^{\top}). (17)

Differentiating and using K≻0K\succ 0 yields

Γ=F​(β​K+α​In)−1=1α​F​(In+βα​K)−1.\Gamma=F(\beta K+\alpha I_{n})^{-1}=\frac{1}{\alpha}F\left(I_{n}+\frac{\beta}{\alpha}K\right)^{-1}. (18)

The indexed kernel gives the same update rule on support points and unseen queries. Consequently g⁡(z)=Γ​kzg(z)=\Gamma k_{z} is exactly Equation 6, and on support points [g⁡(z1),…,g⁡(zn)]=Γ​K=U∗[g(z_{1}),\ldots,g(z_{n})]=\Gamma K=U^{*}. Thus the query formula agrees with the derived support update on the support points.

When is the attention-form approximation accurate?

The resolvent identity and K⪰0K\succeq 0 give

‖u⁡(zq)−α−1​F​kq‖2≤βα2​‖F‖2​‖K‖2​‖kq‖2.\left\|u(z_{q})-\alpha^{-1}Fk_{q}\right\|_{2}\leq\frac{\beta}{\alpha^{2}}\|F\|_{2}\|K\|_{2}\|k_{q}\|_{2}. (19)

Thus β​‖K‖2/α≪1\beta\|K\|_{2}/\alpha\ll 1 controls the absolute remainder relative to the scale ‖F‖2​‖kq‖2/α\|F\|_{2}\|k_{q}\|_{2}/\alpha. This bound motivates the normalized readout and state-dependent scaling in Equation 9.

Appendix C From the Analytic Update to the Implemented Network

We next ask how a network can learn the derived form across tables. Table 3 separates the required computations from our implementation choices. Attention uses learned similarities and contextual values; its normalized output is multiplied by a SiLU gate and projected into a residual correction. This realizes evidence selection, state-dependent scaling, and residual refinement in one block. The gate allows signed, featurewise corrections rather than reconstructing the positive scalar kernel mass s⁡(zq)/αs(z_{q})/\alpha in Equation 8.

Figure 6 shows two additional routes for feature information. Selected feature interaction acts before compression; typed memory later retrieves stored feature states. These components support the architecture in Section 4, while their empirical necessity is assessed by deletion and recovery in Section F.3.

Appendix D Benchmark Protocols and Complete Comparisons

D.1 TabArena v0.1 classification snapshot

The exact 38 datasets are: APSFailure, Amazon employee access, Bank Customer Churn, Bioresponse, Diabetes130US, E-Commerce Shipping Data, Fitness Club, Give Me Some Credit, HR Analytics Job Change, Is-this-a-good-customer, MIC, Marketing Campaign, NATICUSdroid, SDSS17, anneal, bank-marketing, blood-transfusion-service-center, churn, coil2000 insurance policies, credit-g, credit card clients default, customer satisfaction in airline, diabetes, hazelnut-spread contaminant detection, heloc, hiva agnostic, in-vehicle coupon recommendation, jm1, kddcup09 appetency, maternal health risk, online shoppers intention, polish companies bankruptcy, qsar-biodeg, seismic-bumps, splice, students dropout and academic success, taiwanese bankruptcy prediction, and website phishing.

RefineICL uses fold 0, eight ensemble members, and one support ordering shared across model sizes. All 38 datasets are complete. This fixed benchmark snapshot contains 77 reference methods and is not interchangeable with the live leaderboard. The L24 row uses a binary-native continuation at step 20,000, distinct from the L24 checkpoint used for AMLB29. TabArena diagnostics informed this continuation’s prior choice; this is a development-exposed comparison. The separate pure-Stage-2 checkpoint supplies the AMLB29 and extended OpenML results.

D.2 OpenML registries and splits

We save the task data and repeat-0 split assignments before model evaluation. OpenML-CC18 is suite 99 (72 tasks). AMLB29 contains the exact task IDs used by TabPFNv2. The current Grinsztajn classification set combines categorical suite 334 (7 tasks) and numerical suite 337 (16 tasks). Historical22 retains all seven categorical tasks and the fifteen numerical tasks reported by TabPFNv2; Clean18 removes OpenML task 361070 (the numerical eye_movements leakage case), its categorical counterpart, and duplicate datasets. Each result records all views to which it belongs, so overlapping summaries are computed from the same predictions rather than counted as new observations. Canonical TabZilla is suite 379 with 36 tasks. TabZilla102 is a separate, deterministic reconstruction of the official 176-task set using the TabPFNv2 limits and normalized-name deduplication. All ten official folds are saved for every task.

The views overlap and contain 183 unique task IDs in union. We average folds within each task and then tasks within each named benchmark; overlapping memberships are never treated as independent observations.

D.3 Native and common-budget inference

The AMLB29 native protocol follows the archived TabPFNv2 classifier defaults: four estimators, seed 0, temperature 0.9, and a 10,000-row ceiling. We reproduce its multiclass AUC handling. If a test fold omits classes, the corresponding probability columns are removed, the remainder is renormalized, and targets are remapped before OVR-AUC is computed; a two-class remainder uses positive-class ROC-AUC. The extended common-budget panel also uses four estimators: OpenML-CC18 uses seed 42, identical capped support indices, and all 720 folds, while Grinsztajn and TabZilla use seed 0 and their complete registered folds. Query batching may change only the number of queries processed at once; support rows, preprocessing state, feature masks, and ensemble members remain unchanged. Differences in dataset lists and splits motivate separate tables rather than a pooled score.

The AMLB29 TabPFN-v2, PHE, and AutoGluon comparator rows are parsed from the Nature supplement rather than recomputed through an unpinned package constructor. We therefore label the baseline “TabPFN-v2 (Nature default)” throughout; it is not a claim about whichever model a current TabPFN release selects by default.

The current-V3 AMLB29 row is recorded as a direct evaluation with tabpfn==8.0.7 and checkpoint tabpfn-v3-classifier-v3_default.ckpt (SHA-256 d0d865d54dfbc524f5703104be90620182dca7e5fb2c16de72e9959ea18f3988). The checkpoint is loaded from a fixed local path. To isolate model quality from ensemble budget, we use the same four estimators, seed 0, temperature 0.9, 10,000-row support ceiling, folds, and externally materialized data as the other AMLB29 rows. This is the benchmark’s standard four-member comparison, not a claim about the package’s native estimator default. All 290 folds are recorded as complete without failure.

A separate TabICLv2 CC18 reference uses release v2.0.0, eight members, seed 42, and a 10,000-row support ceiling, with 720/720 completed folds. It is reported separately from the four-member panel. A runtime compatibility patch changes two equivalent tuple reductions but not model outputs.

D.4 Available evaluation records

The AMLB29 L12/L24 summaries report 290 complete folds each. Reaggregation of the 290 TabPFN-v3 fold records gives 0.868765 accuracy and 0.936141 OVR-AUC. The L24 AMLB29 checkpoint SHA-256 is 071de368d16d137595d59249a7837d324daf97733acc1d1c5c9f90fd3c5db22b. TabArena uses a later L24 checkpoint (SHA-256 1a96b0ce5f6b1e99a24eb50b65ec20d25af042fd1cae08b196ea7703a5a2e12f). Its 38 per-task outputs and the same 77 reference methods reproduce 1644.8 Elo, 11.078947 mean rank, 0.869105 win rate, and 0.162385 mean error. The six CC18, Grinsztajn, and TabZilla views in Table 2A were also reaggregated from complete ten-fold results for L12, L24, and TabPFN-v3. All records in each view use a single protocol ID and checkpoint hash. The eight-member TabICLv2 CC18 reference is reported separately from these four-member comparisons. The supplement includes archived fold metrics and a script that reconstructs the paired dataset averages in Section D.6, checking task/fold identities, checkpoint hashes, and coverage before aggregation.

D.5 Aggregate benchmark comparisons

The tables below compare RefineICL-L12 and RefineICL-L24 with the current TabPFN-v3 checkpoint under the matched four-member protocols defined in Appendix D. Each number is a dataset-macro mean over the complete registered split set; overlapping benchmark views reuse the same predictions and are not pooled into a single score. The CC18, Grinsztajn, and TabZilla means were recomputed from complete fold results (Section D.4).

The four-member CC18 comparison favors TabPFN-v3 for accuracy and log loss and L24 for OVR-AUC. A separately completed eight-member TabICLv2 v2.0.0 reference reaches 0.88930 accuracy, 0.93864 OVR-AUC and 0.25615 log loss on the same 72-dataset list (720 folds, zero unresolved failures). Its different member budget precludes inclusion in the four-member winner marking.

The Grinsztajn sensitivity views ask whether the observed L24 advantage survives historical membership and leakage/duplicate exclusions. Read each view separately: L24 remains ahead in both metrics, but its Clean18 advantage is only 0.00082 accuracy and 0.00056 AUC. The unadjusted mean differences support consistency of the sign, not a claim of statistical separation.

Canonical36 uses the official TabZilla dataset list; Extension102 checks sensitivity to the separate filtering/deduplication reconstruction. L24 improves all four reported metrics against TabPFN-v3 in both views. The overlapping memberships are not independent replications.

D.6 How broadly are the gains distributed across datasets?

Benchmark means can hide differences in which datasets favor each model. We therefore pair L24 and TabPFN-v3 on the same ten repeat-0 folds, average within each dataset, and compare the resulting dataset scores. All paired dataset and fold identifiers agree. Table 9 reports mean differences and wins/ties/losses; a tie is an absolute difference at most 10−1210^{-12}. We resample whole datasets 20,000 times, retaining the pairing between models and all folds. The 95% percentile intervals describe variation across datasets in each view. They are pointwise intervals, not adjusted for multiple comparisons; overlapping views are analyzed separately, never pooled.

On TabZilla Extension, L24’s mean gains are 0.34 accuracy points [0.09, 0.62] and 0.51 AUC points [0.21, 0.93], with AUC improving on 68 datasets and declining on 17. Canonical AUC improves on 27 datasets and declines on seven, although its mean-difference interval includes zero. CC18 illustrates why the win count and mean answer different questions: accuracy improves on 44 datasets but the mean favors v3, indicating larger losses on some tasks. Grinsztajn Clean18 retains small positive means with intervals spanning zero. Thus the broadest paired evidence here is the TabZilla Extension result, rather than a count of overlapping benchmark means.

Appendix E How Depth, Width, Context, and the FFN Affect the Model

E.1 Do later blocks improve class separation for the current task?

Setup and measured quantity.

Figure 3A uses the pretrained L24 15K checkpoint without parameter updates and a held-out set of 33 class counts (2,4,82,4,8), 33 RBF component counts (4,16,644,16,64), and 88 replicates: 72 episodes, each with 8 features, 1,024 support and 256 query rows. A 256-landmark centered RBF kernel defines equal-energy Gaussian class scores in its first BB nonconstant eigenmodes; query scores use a Nyström extension. The kernel bandwidth is the support-landmark median distance. The held-out seed 805843 changes coordinates, teacher coefficients and labels. Each class must occupy at least 3% of support rows. No probe is fitted to the test episodes.

At each block, normalize row states, average support states within each class, and normalize the resulting prototypes. The two paired measures are the query correct-minus-nearest-wrong cosine margin and nearest-prototype accuracy at block 24 minus block 12. Bootstrap units are the 72 episodes, keeping both layers paired. The margin gain is 0.0509 [0.0403, 0.0616]; the accuracy gain is 2.77 [1.40, 4.02] percentage points. Both support continued class-level refinement. The net improvement from block 12 to block 24 shows stronger class geometry after repeated contextual updates.

E.2 Do the learned block updates improve the support objective?

Figure 3A measures class geometry, but does not directly test the objective that motivates the derivation. We therefore measure Equation 3 immediately before and after each of the 24 contextual blocks of the same L24 checkpoint. This follow-up diagnostic reuses the 72 registered geometry episodes (three class counts, three rule bandwidths, eight replicates), each with 1,024 labeled support rows. We fix τ=1/1024\tau=1/\sqrt{1024} for every layer and task. As a control, we permute a block’s learned support-row updates before adding them to its input states; this retains the set of update vectors but breaks their row assignment. A second control shuffles support labels when evaluating the objective. Neither control changes model parameters or generates a new forward trajectory.

The actual trajectory lowers this support objective, whereas both controls raise it. This links the trained stack to the label-defined geometric target more directly than prototype separation alone. To remove state magnitude as an explanation, we also normalize each support state to unit length and score the same leave-one-out objective with τ=1\tau=1: mean block changes are −0.00458-0.00458 for actual updates and +0.01192+0.01192 for row-permuted updates (72/72 episodes favor the actual assignment). It is not a literal gradient trajectory: the mean cosine between a block update and the negative objective gradient is only 0.00710.0071, and some blocks raise the objective. The result identifies a stack-level effect on this surrogate, not the exact operator in Equation 4.

Does a learned support write matter to the query prediction? In a separate paired intervention on the same episodes, we keep block 12’s query output unchanged but replace its support output with its input, then run the remaining blocks normally. We score cross-entropy over the task’s CC class logits. Skipping that one support write raises final query CE by 0.0510 on average (episode-bootstrap 95% CI [0.0417, 0.0608]; 72/72 episodes) and lowers query accuracy by 1.44 points. The intervention shows a causal contribution of the mid-stack support write to query prediction. It does not establish that the leave-one-out objective mediates that contribution: after centering within each of the nine class-count/rule-bandwidth cells, the Spearman correlation between block-12 objective reduction and query-CE benefit is −0.026-0.026. The supplement includes the paired episode records, probe drivers, and policies.

E.3 Do broader rules use more representation dimensions?

Setup and measured quantity.

Figure 3B fixes the same L24 checkpoint, eight features, 1,024 support rows and 256 queries. The teacher construction above varies only B∈{2,4,8,16,32,64,128}B\in\{2,4,8,16,32,64,128\} across three class counts and six replicates (seed 805742). A single rank-32 PCA basis, calibrated on disjoint episodes, projects the 1,024-dimensional contextual state after block 4; all later blocks remain unchanged. The primary comparison is the bottleneck loss at B=64B=64 minus that at B=4B=4 within each of the 18 class-count/replicate units. Full-state accuracy must exceed chance by 10 points in every primary bandwidth-by-class cell; this validity check passes.

Table 11 reports all seven rule sizes. Read the increase in full-minus-projected accuracy loss, not raw hidden rank. The primary increase is 7.62 [6.03, 9.05] points. The result shows task-dependent use of representation dimensions within this checkpoint; retraining a smaller-width network could compensate. The smallest and largest rule sizes extend the original comparison; they are not additional main tests. Within the selected BB kernel modes, label r90r_{90} counts the leading modes accounting for 90% of the projected, centered one-hot label energy; its denominator excludes the remaining modes.

E.4 Does additional distinct evidence change the architecture gap?

Setup and measured quantity.

Figure 3C uses L12 at 40K and L24 at 15K. The experiment has three boundary families (checkerboard, rings, wave), six frequencies (2,4,6,8,10,122,4,6,8,10,12) and four replicates, for 72 paired conditions (seed 804815). Coordinates lie in [−3,3]2[-3,3]^{2}. Each condition fixes 512 queries in a boundary band of width 0.2 and a shared set of 1,024 support rows; nested prefixes of 128, 192, 256, 384, 512, 768 and 1,024 rows contain no duplicates.

The primary measure is the change in the L24-minus-L12 accuracy gap between 128 and 1,024 rows, with bootstrap resampling of all 72 paired conditions. The 4.01 [2.26, 5.79]-point interaction supports an increasing overall architecture advantage with evidence. It is not pointwise monotone: the gap decreases from 1.02 points at 192 rows to 0.75 at 256. The checkpoints differ in depth, width, and training history, so this experiment isolates the effect of evidence on their gap, not an isolated effect of depth or parameter count.

E.5 Is an expanded FFN needed at a fixed training budget?

The question is whether omitting an expanded FFN prevents competitive prediction when optimization opportunity is held fixed. Table 12 reports the complete six-cell d=96d=96 depth-by-FFN experiment after the same 100K training updates. All cells use RowCLS8, 512-row episodes (30–90% labeled support), global batch 32, the official GraphSCM-v2 Stage-1 classification prior, contextual gating, feature interaction, typed memory, and the same optimizer and validation protocol. The global FFN setting changes the column, row, and contextual blocks together. They share one training seed (42); these are single-seed results, not averages over independent training runs. The reported result is held-out GraphSCM-v2 validation, separate from the public benchmarks and the fixed-checkpoint boundary-rule evaluation below.

At this budget, L4 no-FFN is within 0.00175 CE of L8 FFN-2×\times. The FFN effect depends on depth: it worsens CE at L2 and L4 but improves it at L8; at L2, CE and accuracy favor different variants. The L4 no-FFN model nearly matches the L8 FFN model’s CE with a smaller contextual stack.

E.6 How much accuracy does the FFN buy at each memory cost?

We measure the prediction–memory trade-off of whole-model FFN expansion using the paired d=96d=96, eight-block models at 100K updates. The pair shares the initialization seed, GraphSCM-v2 episode stream, optimizer, eight RowCLS tokens, contextual gating, feature-interaction modules, typed memory, and 512-row training episodes with a 30–90% support fraction. The shared training seed is 42; optimization uses Muon, peak learning rate 8×10−48\times 10^{-4}, 500 warmup steps and cosine decay to 8×10−58\times 10^{-5}. A global factor of zero or two disables or enables FFNs in all six column-attention subblocks, three row-encoder blocks, and eight contextual blocks. This compares whole-model FFN expansion, not a contextual-only intervention. Total parameters increase from 30,934,796 to 50,154,956 (+62.1%): 222,336 are added to the column encoder, 111,168 to the row encoder, and 18,886,656 to the contextual predictor. The supplement includes an executable parameter audit. Measured memory also includes runtime allocations.

We keep both checkpoints unchanged and evaluate three boundary-rule families, six frequencies and three replicates (54 paired conditions, seed 806031), with 384 fixed boundary-band queries per condition, at seven nested context sizes, n∈{128,192,256,384,512,768,1024}n\in\{128,192,256,384,512,768,1024\}. Every added row is a distinct labeled observation; no row is duplicated to equalize token count. For each condition, the support and query coordinates, labels, and nesting order are identical across models. Memory is measured on an NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB, with FP32 model weights and FP16 autocast, one episode per forward pass, and all 384 queries in one batch. We use the raw tensor forward path, no ensemble, zero dropout, and no gradient recording or activation recomputation. Before each measurement we reset the CUDA peak-memory counter; the reported maximum allocated memory includes resident weights and temporary tensors, not reserved allocator memory. Paired bootstrap intervals resample the 54 conditions.

Figure 7 shows the complete result underlying Table 2B. At 1,024 rows, the expanded FFN improves accuracy by 1.11 points (95% CI [0.38,1.89][0.38,1.89]), while increasing peak memory by 60.2%. Both models improve strongly with distinct evidence: 18.60 points without the expanded FFN and 19.95 points with it. The FFN also increases the 128–1,024 evidence gain by 1.35 points [0.26, 2.45]. Thus it can improve evidence use, while the no-FFN model already scales strongly. These paired-episode intervals condition on a single training seed and do not measure variability across training runs.

Appendix F How Support Labels and Queries Control the Update

F.1 Do support labels select a different predictor?

Figure 5 shows the predictions summarized by the heatmap in Figure 4B. With L24 parameters unchanged and identical support/query coordinates, only support labels change among linear, XOR, radial and wave rules. The output is the predicted class-1 probability surface; the black generating boundary provides the reference. Matching-rule accuracy averages 0.98498 versus 0.51475 against other rules. Thus, on the same point cloud, the support labels determine which predictor the model uses.

F.2 Does each query need its own attention output and gate?

The question is whether each correction must reach the query for which it was computed (Figure 4A). The experiment uses the pretrained L24 step-15K checkpoint without parameter updates and a separate paired RBF episode set. Each context size contains 54 tasks spanning three class counts, three RBF component counts, and six replicates; every condition receives exactly the same support features, labels, queries, and targets. In the evidence-mismatch condition, attention outputs are permuted across query tokens while gates and residual states remain fixed. In the gate-mismatch condition, gate preactivations are permuted while routed evidence and residual states remain fixed. In the matched-update condition, evidence and gate preactivation receive the same permutation, preserving their pairing while assigning the resulting update to the wrong residual state. Every permutation preserves the set of vectors within the query segment. Table 13 reports accuracy loss relative to the unchanged model, with paired 95% bootstrap intervals.

All three damage intervals remain positive at every context size. Even keeping the evidence–gate pair intact does not rescue the wrong-recipient update, showing that updates are query-specific.

F.3 Can the remaining components compensate after deletion?

Which components does the trained model depend on, and which recover after brief adaptation? All conditions start from L24 at 15K. Direct deletion is evaluated at step 0; recovery keeps the deletion, loads weights only, resets Muon optimizer state, and uses the same GraphSCM-v2 stream for 250 updates (learning rate 10−410^{-4}, global batch 8, seed 918273). The unmodified reference receives the same continuation. We report all three planned checkpoints (25, 100, and 250 updates).

The typed-frontend tests set one or both pre-compression residuals to zero; the row-FI tests set the row-encoder adapters to zero and keep them fixed. The memory tests remove one or both reads. The gate test replaces all 24 SiLU gate outputs with one while preserving attention, normalization, projection and residual writes. These operations measure component dependence in a trained model, not from-scratch architectural necessity.

Table 14 gives the full RBF results. Most individual frontend and row-FI changes stay near zero, whereas removing both memory reads continues to hurt and the gate effect remains large after recovery. At 250 updates, removing the gate, memory, and row FI together costs 42.54 points, compared with 28.94 for the gate alone. This identifies an additional effect of jointly removing memory and row FI; their individual effects are much smaller.

The real-table check reuses 12 model-independent, non-TabArena OpenML-CC18 tasks, four fixed support/query splits per task, 409 distinct support rows, and 128 queries. Inputs are byte-identical across conditions. Because this check was designed after observing the RBF results, it tests whether the main effects also appear on real tables; it is not a second test specified in advance. Intervals resample tasks while retaining all four splits.

Table 15 gives the per-dataset effects after matched recovery. It distinguishes broad component dependence from effects concentrated on particular tables: gate deletion hurts all 12 datasets, whereas row-FI deletion has its largest effect on Madelon (OpenML 1485). The supplement provides both recovery endpoints, split-level scores, and input hashes, with a script that reconstructs this table and checks the means in Figure 8.

Appendix G Boundary Conditions for the Refinement Account

G.1 Does better execution imply better sparse rule identification?

This test asks whether scaling helps every part of rule learning. The weights and coordinates are fixed while the labeling function varies over a fixed set of candidate rules. Sixteen rules in each of three complexity families share 1,024 support and 2,048 query coordinates. With 32 or 128 independent rows, repeated rows fill 1,024 support positions. The decoder selects the rule within each family whose target has minimum cross-entropy to the predicted surface; the label-blind top-1 ceiling is 1/161/16. Balanced random labels preserve class counts and recover 3/48 rules in total, the pooled chance count.

Read retrieval as rule identification and own-rule query CE as prediction quality in Figure 9. At 32 independent rows L12 retrieves 39/48 rules and L24 32/48. At 128 rows both reach 48/48; L24 then has lower own-rule query CE by 0.02329, and by 0.00842 and 0.01557 at 512 and 1,024 rows. The larger-depth checkpoint therefore does not uniformly identify sparse rules better. Repetition holds support positions fixed but changes multiplicity; this is a unique-evidence control, not a substitute for the distinct-prefix experiment in Section E.4.

G.2 Does a rule found early disappear in later layers?

To test whether later layers lose a rule that was already found, we reuse the 16-rule low-, medium-, and high-complexity families specified in advance, identical support and query coordinates, 2,048 query rows, and the same 32-row repetition order as the evidence sweep. Every layer is decoded through the shared final normalization and head. Rule retrieval is computed within each family, so a label-blind output has a 1/161/16 ceiling. We ask whether retrieval falls by at least two rules from its best intermediate layer to the final layer, or whether the missing rule was never recovered at any layer.

The primary criterion is a drop of at least two rules from the best layer to the final layer. L24 never exceeds its final 32/48 retrieval, while L12 ends at 39/48; the observed layerwise result therefore rejects late loss of a rule that was already decodable. A different intermediate readout could still recover additional information. Cross-checkpoint differences can also reflect width, frontend and training history.

G.3 Can response rank be high when task performance is poor?

The response-rank experiment fixes 128 distinct support coordinates, repeats them to 1,024 positions in one shared order, and uses 512 fixed query coordinates. Sixteen Fourier rules in each of three families supply 48 target surfaces. Coherent and class-count-preserving shuffled labels share the same inputs. Hidden query responses are flattened, and spectral measures use their 48×4848\times 48 Gram matrix. We remove each response’s spatial mean and normalize its norm before centering across rules. Retrieval uses cross-entropy against the 48 targets, and CKA compares response and target geometries.

Figure 11 should be read jointly: final outputs from the true labels retrieve 47/48 rules for both checkpoints, whereas shuffled L12 and L24 retrieve 1/48 and 0/48 despite sometimes higher effective rank. Thus raw rank alone does not measure task performance, which motivates the controlled rank limit in Section E.3. This 512-query, 48-way retrieval probe differs from the 2,048-query within-family rule set, so its counts are not pooled.

G.4 Does a layerwise readout approach a known prediction target?

As a complementary target-space check, we generate 64 binary logistic episodes whose conditional distribution is known exactly. Applying the shared final normalization and decoder at every L24 block gives a layerwise predictor pe,ℓp_{e,\ell}. Its Bayes excess cross-entropy falls from 0.13047 at block 0 to 0.02559 at block 12 and 0.01476 at block 24. Blocks 13–24 therefore remove another 0.01082 excess cross-entropy (paired episode-bootstrap 95% interval [0.00858, 0.01311]). A support-only logistic ERM reaches 0.01416 and serves only as a finite-sample reference. This known-generator result agrees with the class-prototype intervention in the main text while relying on a narrower binary task family.

The solver probe uses 64 paired episodes, 256 support rows, 512 query rows, and feature dimension in {2,4,8}\{2,4,8\}. Every state is decoded through the final normalization and head; final decoded logits reproduce production logits within 10−310^{-3}. Affine-logit readout R2R^{2} is 0.97745 for L12 and 0.98770 for L24.

Intervals resample episodes. Cross-checkpoint differences are not depth-only, and the candidate optimizer directions are too similar to identify a unique internal optimizer. This supports later-block progress toward a known target, without identifying a unique internal optimization algorithm.

Appendix H Scope, Limitations, and Reproducibility

Analytic and learned updates.

The proof concerns a locally smooth leave-one-out support objective with at least two examples per class. The kernel approximation requires small β​‖K‖2/α\beta\|K\|_{2}/\alpha; neither its exact gradient nor its scale is computed explicitly by the network. Query risk and repeated learned-block descent are empirical questions, not consequences of the proposition.

Scope of the interventions.

Mechanism tests emphasize synthetic classification with known rules. The real-table recovery panel tests a narrower transfer claim. A shared final decoder can miss intermediate information, and disabling components at inference can create states not encountered during training. Short recovery does not replace training all ablated architectures to convergence. The fixed-budget FFN grid has one training seed; paired episode intervals do not quantify training variance.

What scale comparisons establish.

L12 and L24 differ in depth, width, and training history. The change in their accuracy gap with context size therefore applies only to this pair of checkpoints. The rank-32 projection measures sensitivity inside one trained model. The sparse-rule deficit and intermediate reversals rule out uniform improvement with additional depth or context. Parameter ratios against TabFM are storage comparisons; they do not establish a matched-compute training advantage.

Benchmark and release scope.

Section D.4 records which headline results were reaggregated from task or fold outputs and identifies the distinct L24 checkpoints used by AMLB29 and TabArena. The TabArena ranking belongs to the fixed 38-dataset, fold-0 snapshot and its heterogeneous reference budgets. Overlapping OpenML views and metrics are not independent trials, and small mean differences alone do not establish statistical superiority. Complete RefineICL TALENT evaluations are unavailable in the reported evidence and do not enter a comparison. Regression is outside scope. The code supplement contains the model, synthetic priors, training loop, optimizer, and JSON recipes, plus focused tests and a CPU smoke run. It documents the benchmark-checkpoint mapping and training stages. Trained weights, benchmark data, and the real-informed continuation manifests are not included; the supplied source therefore supports model construction and synthetic training rather than a complete replay of the TabArena continuation.
